title: Socrates and Xanthippe: After Thunder Comes the Rain!
culture_region: India / Greece / USA / South Africa / World
summary: When Xanthippe berated Socrates and dumped a bucket of dirty water over his head, the philosopher calmly remarked: 'Did I not say that Xanthippe's thunder would end in rain?'
keywords: Socrates and Xanthippe: After Thunder Comes the Rain!
full_text:
While Socrates was celebrated as the wisest mind of Greece, his domestic life was notoriously turbulent. His wife Xanthippe was legendary for her fiery temper, driven to despair by her husband's indifference to money and his habit of spending all day conversing in the agora.

One morning, Socrates was seated outside his doorstep, engaged in a philosophical dialogue with his disciples.

Frustrated by the family's empty pantry, Xanthippe burst onto the porch and unleashed a torrent of fierce scolding, berating Socrates as a useless idler who cared for the whole world except his own household.

Socrates sat with serene, Buddha-like composure, not uttering a word of anger.

Infuriated by his placid smile, Xanthippe marched upstairs, seized a heavy bucket of dirty wash water, and dumped it directly over Socrates' head!

Muddy water soaked his beard, his tunic, and splashed his astonished disciples.

Socrates wiped the water from his eyes, turned toward his horrified students with an affectionate chuckle, and remarked:

**"Did I not warn you, friends, that after all that thunder from Xanthippe, rain was sure to follow?"**

The porch erupted in laughter, and Xanthippe retreated inside, disarmed by his humor.

When asked why he chose such a challenging spouse, Socrates replied:
"Trainers of horses choose the most spirited steeds, for if they can master them, they can manage any horse. Living with Xanthippe has taught me to remain calm in the face of any hostility from mankind!"
moral: Patience and good humor are the ultimate shields against domestic anger and external provocation.
